content: Calcium carbonate is indicated for the relief of heartburn, acid indigestion, sour stomach, or upset stomach associated with these symptoms. It is also used in the treatment of hyperphosphatemia in patients with end-stage renal disease. Dosages vary depending on the condition and age group, with specific recommendations for children and adults. Over-the-counter (OTC) products may have varying approved uses and age restrictions, so it is essential to consult product-specific labeling for details. Calcium carbonate interacts with numerous medications, often by altering gastric pH or through cation binding in the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. These interactions can lead to decreased absorption or efficacy of certain drugs, or in some cases, increased drug levels or effects. Below are detailed descriptions of these interactions: 1. Ceftriaxone and Calcium Carbonate: Co-administration of calcium-containing solutions (e.g., Ringer or Hartmann solutions) with intravenous ceftriaxone is contraindicated due to the risk of potentially fatal particulate precipitation in the lungs and kidneys. Separate administration by at least 48 hours. 2. Atazanavir: Calcium carbonate increases gastric pH, reducing atazanavir solubility and plasma concentrations. Administer atazanavir 2 hours before or 1 hour after calcium carbonate. 3. Baloxavir Marboxil: Calcium carbonate binds to polyvalent cations in the GI tract, reducing baloxavir absorption. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. 4. Dapsone: Calcium carbonate increases gastric pH, reducing dapsone levels. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. 5. Dasatinib: Calcium carbonate increases gastric pH, reducing dasatinib levels. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. 6. Demeclocycline: Calcium carbonate inhibits GI absorption of demeclocycline. Separate administration by 2 hours. 7. Digoxin: Calcium carbonate increases gastric pH, potentially increasing digoxin levels. Monitor closely for adverse effects. 8. Doxycycline: Calcium carbonate inhibits GI absorption of doxycycline. Separate administration by 2 hours. 9. Eltrombopag: Calcium carbonate inhibits GI absorption of eltrombopag. Separate administration by at least 4 hours. 10. Erdafitinib: Avoid co-administration during the initial dosing adjustment period (first 21 days) due to pharmacodynamic effects on serum phosphate levels. 11. Indinavir: Calcium carbonate increases gastric pH, reducing indinavir levels. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. 12. Infigratinib: Calcium carbonate inhibits GI absorption of infigratinib. Administer infigratinib 2 hours before and after locally-acting antacids. 13. Ketoconazole and Levoketoconazole: Calcium carbonate increases gastric pH, reducing ketoconazole levels. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. 14. Minocycline: Calcium carbonate inhibits GI absorption of minocycline. Separate administration by 2 hours. 15. Nimodipine, Nisoldipine, and Nitrendipine: Calcium carbonate increases gastric pH, potentially increasing the levels of these drugs. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. 16. Oxytetracycline: Calcium carbonate inhibits GI absorption of oxytetracycline. Separate administration by 2 hours. 17. Pazopanib: Calcium carbonate increases gastric pH, reducing pazopanib solubility. Avoid co-administration with drugs that raise gastric pH. 18. Ponatinib: Calcium carbonate increases gastric pH, reducing ponatinib levels. Avoid co-administration or use an alternative drug. 19. Sotorasib: Calcium carbonate inhibits GI absorption of sotorasib. Administer sotorasib 4 hours before or 10 hours after locally-acting antacids. 20. Tetracycline: Calcium carbonate inhibits GI absorption of tetracycline. Separate administration by 2 hours. 21. Acalabrutinib: Calcium carbonate increases gastric pH, reducing acalabrutinib solubility. Separate administration by at least 2 hours. 22. Acebutolol: Calcium carbonate inhibits GI absorption of acebutolol. Separate administration by 2 hours. 23. Alendronate: Calcium carbonate inhibits GI absorption of alendronate. Separate administration by 30 minutes. 24. Allopurinol: Calcium carbonate inhibits GI absorption of allopurinol. Separate administration by 2 hours. 25. Amantadine: Calcium carbonate may lead to amantadine accumulation due to urine alkalinization. Monitor for adverse effects. 26. Amlodipine: Calcium carbonate may antagonize the pharmacodynamic effects of amlodipine. Monitor closely. 27. Amphetamine: Calcium carbonate increases amphetamine levels through passive renal tubular reabsorption. Monitor closely. 28. Atenolol: Calcium carbonate inhibits GI absorption of atenolol. Separate administration by 2 hours. 29. Azithromycin: Calcium carbonate inhibits GI absorption of azithromycin. Separate administration by 2 hours. 30. Bearberry: Calcium carbonate increases bearberry levels through passive renal tubular reabsorption. Monitor closely. 31. Benazepril: Calcium carbonate may reduce benazepril effects through an unspecified mechanism. Monitor closely. 32. Benzphetamine: Calcium carbonate increases benzphetamine levels through passive renal tubular reabsorption. Monitor closely. 33. Betaxolol: Calcium carbonate inhibits GI absorption of betaxolol. Separate administration by 2 hours. 34. Bictegravir: Calcium carbonate binds to bictegravir in the GI tract, reducing its levels. Administer bictegravir 2 hours before or with food. 35. Bisoprolol: Calcium carbonate inhibits GI absorption of bisoprolol. Separate administration by 2 hours. 36. Bosutinib: Calcium carbonate increases gastric pH, reducing bosutinib solubility. Use short-acting antacids and separate administration by 2 hours. 37. Budesonide: Calcium carbonate increases gastric pH, potentially causing premature dissolution of extended-release budesonide tablets. Monitor closely. 38. Cabotegravir: Calcium carbonate binds to cabotegravir in the GI tract, reducing its levels. Administer antacids 2 hours before or 4 hours after cabotegravir. 39. Captopril: Calcium carbonate may reduce captopril absorption. Monitor closely. 40. Carbonyl Iron: Calcium carbonate increases gastric pH, reducing carbonyl iron levels. Monitor closely. 41. Carvedilol: Calcium carbonate inhibits GI absorption of carvedilol. Separate administration by 2 hours. 42. Cefdinir, Cefditoren, Cefpodoxime, and Cefuroxime: Calcium carbonate increases gastric pH, reducing the levels of these cephalosporins. Monitor closely. 43. Celecoxib: Calcium carbonate inhibits GI absorption of celecoxib. Separate administration by 2 hours. 44. Celiprolol: Calcium carbonate inhibits GI absorption of celiprolol. Separate administration by 2 hours. 45. Chenodiol: Calcium carbonate inhibits GI absorption of chenodiol. Separate administration by 2 hours. 46. Chloroquine: Calcium carbonate binds to chloroquine in the GI tract, reducing its levels. Separate doses by at least 4 hours. 47. Ciprofloxacin: Calcium carbonate inhibits GI absorption of ciprofloxacin. Administer ciprofloxacin 2 hours before or 6 hours after calcium salts. 48. Clevidipine: Calcium carbonate may antagonize the pharmacodynamic effects of clevidipine. Monitor closely. 49. Crizotinib: Calcium carbonate increases gastric pH, reducing crizotinib solubility. Monitor closely. 50. Cyclosporine: Calcium carbonate inhibits GI absorption of cyclosporine. Separate administration by 2 hours. 51. Dabrafenib: Calcium carbonate increases gastric pH, reducing dabrafenib solubility. Monitor closely. 52. Deferiprone: Calcium carbonate binds to deferiprone in the GI tract. Separate administration by at least 4 hours. 53. Deferoxamine: Deferoxamine may reduce calcium carbonate levels by chelation. Monitor closely. 54. Delafloxacin: Calcium carbonate binds to delafloxacin in the GI tract. Administer delafloxacin 2 hours before or 6 hours after calcium carbonate. 55. Dextroamphetamine: Calcium carbonate increases dextroamphetamine levels through passive renal tubular reabsorption. Monitor closely. 56. Digoxin: Calcium carbonate may synergistically increase digoxin effects. Monitor closely. 57. Diltiazem: Calcium carbonate may antagonize the pharmacodynamic effects of diltiazem. Monitor closely. 58. Dolutegravir: Calcium carbonate binds to dolutegravir in the GI tract. Administer dolutegravir 2 hours before or 6 hours after calcium carbonate. 59. Elvitegravir: Calcium carbonate binds to elvitegravir in the GI tract, reducing its levels. Monitor closely. This list highlights the importance of carefully managing drug interactions with calcium carbonate to ensure therapeutic efficacy and minimize adverse effects.
